While this goal followed the SMARTER structure on paper, in practice I did not genuinely follow through on the evaluate and review components. The goals were written as part of the session requirement rather than as an active framework guiding my training decisions. This is a significant weakness because without genuine evaluation there was no structured way to identify that my feet abduction was worsening across sessions rather than improving, which was directly impacting my ability to keep my COM within my BOS and sustain the hold. The class material "Skill Acquisition Stages" notes that performers at the associative stage benefit most from being encouraged to self-analyse their errors (2). A properly applied SMARTER goal targeting gluteus medius engagement specifically would have directed my attention toward this weakness far earlier and shaped my individual practice time in later sessions around correcting it. Goal setting therefore had minimal impact on my actual learning progression, and the biomechanical improvements I made were driven almost entirely by internal feedback and Ignacio's external advice rather than any structured psychological framework.
The connection between all of these principles runs throughout the entire learning process. The wrist corrections in the execution phase depend on the COG being close enough to the BOS to be corrected. The COG is only there if the kick up momentum was calibrated correctly through force summation. Calibrating that momentum required transitioning out of the cognitive stage through appropriate distributed and massed practice across the nine sessions. And genuine SMARTER goal setting would have accelerated that transition by identifying specific anatomical weaknesses earlier. My improvement from legs barely leaving the floor in the pretest to a consistent five second freestanding hold reflects how each of these principles built on one another progressively.

Section 1 – Goals
By the end of the session after the next, I want to be able to perform the handstand skill with fully extended arms, adducted legs and plantarflexed feet for at least three seconds without any external physical assistance. This goal is specific by targeting the key criteria of a great handstand taught within the course. It is measurable as success is clearly defined by holding the position for a countable duration. It is also achievable as I have already begun developing foundation movements in previous sessions, making a brief unassisted hold a realistic next step. It is timebound to the upcoming session. I will evaluate my progress by reflecting on whether or not I was able to sustain the hold and identify any errors, and I will review it at the start of the following session to determine whether the goal needs to be adjusted. It is worth noting that a handstand is classified as an excellence skill, placing it well beyond the scope of what is formally required within the course. However, I want to extend myself by going for a handstand pushup as a personal long term target beyond the curriculum.
By the end of the next session, I aim to complete a full cartwheel passing through a straight upside-down position with fully extended arms on at least four out of five attempts. This goal is specific by targeting the most common error I currently make while performing the cartwheel skill. It is measurable through the success rate across five attempts, which is quantifiable. It is achievable as it represents a small but meaningful progression from my current level without expecting full mastery. It is relevant as the cartwheel is the fundamental skill within the course that leads to many more advanced movements. It is also timebound to the next session. I will evaluate it by reflecting on the coach's feedback during the session and will review it afterwards to consider whether I am ready to begin progressing towards the associative stage.
Section 2 – Critical Analysis
While both goals follow the SMARTER structure on paper, in practice I did not genuinely follow through on the evaluate and review components. The goals were written as part of the session requirement rather than as an active framework guiding my training decisions. This is a significant weakness because without genuine evaluation there was no structured way to identify that my feet abduction was worsening across sessions rather than improving, which was directly impacting my ability to keep my COM within my BOS and sustain the hold. According to the class material on skill acquisition, performers at the associative stage benefit most from being encouraged to self-analyse their errors, meaning genuine SMARTER goal evaluation would have been particularly valuable at exactly the stage I was at. If I had genuinely reviewed the handstand goal at the start of each session, I would have been able to set progressively specific targets around the gluteus medius engagement, which was the anatomical cause of the feet abduction, and structured my individual practice time in later sessions around correcting it. This would likely have extended my hold beyond five seconds and reduced the lateral displacement of my COM earlier in the course. Goal setting therefore had minimal impact on my actual learning progression, and the biomechanical improvements I did make were driven almost entirely by internal feedback and Ignacio's external advice rather than any structured psychological framework.
